title: Live: Blues bite back after horror start in must-win clash against Suns
text:

Later on today, Hawthorn faces Essendon at the MCG from 4:15pm, while the GWS Giants take on Sydney at the Showgrounds from 4:35pm.

In this evening's final match, the Western Bulldogs host Richmond at Docklands Stadium from 7:40pm (all times AEST).

title: 'Blight on the sport': Fight cancelled on Tszyu card after weigh-in
text:
Luckless Australian boxer Liam Wilson has been dealt another cruel blow, with his scheduled world title eliminator against Stephen Fulton cancelled after the American failed to make weight.

In farcical scenes, Fulton hit the scales at almost 63.5kg on Saturday, almost 4.5kg more than the two-division world champion was originally supposed to fight Wilson at in Sydney.

Fulton and Wilson were supposed to square off at the super-featherweight of 59kg before officials on Friday raised the weight to 60.3kg for the feature bout on the blockbuster Tim Tszyu-Errol Spence Jr card.

Wilson had happily agreed to the late change, saying he was desperate to earn another world title shot with a victory over the former unified super-bantamweight world champion and ex-WBC featherweight belt holder.

But now the American's team is being accused of never truly intending to fight on Sunday.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

"This feels like a stitch-up," Wilson's manager and Tszyu's ex-agent Glenn Jennings said.

"If you are serious and you sign a contract at 133 [pounds], there is an expectation that you will deliver.

"It is not only unacceptable, it is a blight on the sport. This is unprofessional, there is nowhere to go for this bloke now."

Undefeated Olympian Paulo Aokuso will move to the main card, taking on Luis Tejeda from the Dominican Republic in a light-heavyweight bout.

Wilson's fight is the second co-main event to be cancelled this week after Fulton's fellow American Jermall Charlo was denied a visa to face rising Australian Koen Mazoudier.

title: 'We can all feel it': Bronze medal lifts Aussie gymnasts' outlook
text:
Australian gymnast Jesse Moore had a sinking feeling in his stomach: he had seen this movie before.

Four years ago at the Commonwealth Games in Birmingham, the nation's best male artistic gymnasts fell agonisingly short of bronze by 0.650 points after slipping at the death to Cyprus.

Fast forward to Glasgow and Australia found themselves in a similar position when hosts Scotland mounted a late challenge en route to the final of six apparatuses.

With just one point the difference in the men's final at Glasgow International Stadium, Australia's five-man squad withstood the raucous home crowd and proved their mettle on the pommel horse to avoid history repeating.

Bolstered by a strong start on rings and horizontal bar, Australia clinched bronze with a combined score of 235.650 points.

A near-flawless Canada team won gold (241.400 points), pipping 2022 Birmingham champions England by 3.150 points.

Australia's men won their first team medal since their maiden gold at the 2010 Delhi Games, doing so with four debutants in the five-man squad.

Paris Olympian Moore was the only Australian man to have experience on the Games stage, leading Ritam Malik, James Hardy, Ben Foster and Tru Hagens.

Australia's Ritam Malik flips through the air after performing on the rings. (Getty Images: Jane Barlow/PA Images)

Moore, 23, laughed when asked if his mind went back to the 2022 Games.

"You always have that in the back of your mind," Moore said.

"But we have got a job to do. The game's not over yet.

"The way we finished on pommel is pretty extraordinary. It shows how well we've come over the past few years.

"It's a bit weird being one of the oldest and most experienced on the team. I'm proud to be that in this team.

"We're certainly on track, only upwards from here.

"We can all feel it and people back home can feel it as well."

Moore notched Australia's second-best score (13.300) on the apparatus behind Malik (13.500), while 19-year-old Hagens was awarded 13.100 points despite falling.

Pommel horse specialist Hagens had waited through the nearly four-hour final for his only apparatus.

Australia claims six gold on Commonwealth Games opening day Australia claims six gold medals, and 13 overall, to open competition on day one of the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow.

Hagens started his 40-second cameo just as Scotland began their last-ditch effort for the podium on the horizontal bar.

Cameron Lynn (13.500) and Reuben Ward (13.150) matched it with the Australians, but crowd favourite Hamish Carter scored 12.900 points.

"I was pretty nervous," Hagens said.

"Not the outcome I wanted, but it was good to get up there, finish it off for the team, to get up a score we needed to get the medal."

A horrific injury to English gymnast Gabriel Langton put a damper on the final.

Langton had to be stretchered from the Glasgow International Arena after falling from the horizontal bar and landing on his head and neck, resulting in a 15-minute pause in competition.

The 19-year-old lay motionless on the ground for several minutes, but gave a thumbs up as he left the arena.

title: RFDS brings Australian-first care to remote Gulf community
text:
After years of widening health gaps, a remote Gulf community has taken control of its own health care in an Australian-first move designed to improve lives and stem mounting youth suicides.

Data released by Mornington Island Council shows nearly 40 per cent of the 1,200 residents in the Gulf of Carpentaria community of Mornington Island are living with one or more chronic diseases.

Mornington Island is located off the coast of the Gulf of Carpentaria, and is only accessible via plane or ferry. (ABC Northwest: Antoinette Raffau)

With more than 80 per cent of the population being Indigenous, the data also reveals the community's death rate remains significantly higher than the rest of Queensland, at more than 40 per cent.

In a push to buck the trend, community advocacy group the Ngarnal Aboriginal Community Controlled Health Service took over primary healthcare delivery on the Island last month, with clinical care to be delivered through the Royal Flying Doctor Service (RFDS).

Ngarnal Aboriginal Community Controlled Health Service opened its doors in July. (Supplied: Ngarnal Aboriginal Community Controlled Health Service)

Ngarnal chair Susan Sewter said, in previous decades, health care on the island, more than 1,860 kilometres north-west of Brisbane, had consistently failed residents.

"We need to be able to be in control of our health," Ms Sewter said.

"We've got to be healthy to be able to participate in education, employment and training in the community in general.

"We've relied on everyone else up until now. It's time for us to step up and make this work for us."

The delivery model, split between the two organisations, will be the first of its kind in Australia.

Ms Sewter said previous providers relied on locums and offered limited services, meaning residents were less willing to seek health care.

She said the new system promised permanent, long-term staff on the island.

A rotating team of RFDS doctors and nurses provide healthcare, with the Ngarnal Community Clinic team. (Supplied: Yvonne Doveren)

"One of the major things that we looked at is we needed to have consistency in the medical service," Ms Sewter said.

"That means the same doctors, the same nurses so our community can build a relationship with a medical team."

The model would see RFDS deliver clinical care on the island for the next two years, when the parties could renegotiate.

'Unique' model has replication potential

RFDS Primary Healthcare Medical Lead Yvonne Doveren said staff would work on rotating five-day rosters to ensure one doctor, two nurses and an Aboriginal health practitioner were on the island each week.

"It's unique in that we have this partnership with an Aboriginal community-controlled health service," Dr Doveren said.

Yvonne Doveren says rotating staff will fly into Mornington Island ensuring consistent care each week. (ABC News: Abbey Halter)

"The people of Mornington Island are slowly coming into the clinic, and we are still building connections … which is, of course, always the most important part of primary health care.

"We hope that with this new clinic, we can welcome the people of Mornington Island, share a cup of tea while they wait to see the doctors and the nurses, and basically provide really solid, good primary health care."

Dr Doveren said this style of health care was critical for remote parts of the state.

Yvonne Doveren says the collaboration aims to improve the overall wellbeing of residents. (ABC News: Abbey Halter)

"We provide primary health care in a lot of Queensland health facilities but, in this case, it's a new model of care," she said.

" I think it's a model that could be applied in lots of areas in Queensland. "

Community-led importance

University of Queensland senior research fellow at the Poche Centre for Indigenous Health, and a Narungga and Ngarrindjeri man, Stephen Harfield said community-led care provided better health outcomes for mob.

"We know that culture is really central to that component of delivering care," Dr Harfield said.

Stephen Harfield says community led care in remote Aboriginal regions can improve health outcomes. (Supplied: Dr Stephen Harfield)

"Being able to receive care from your local community, from people who know your community and understand the impacts of living in such a remote community and understand the broader context in terms of health and wellbeing needs."

He said the walk-in aspect of the clinic, allowing accessible care for the community, could positively impact how residents engaged with their health and wellbeing.

"If this partnership between RFDS and Ngarnal is successful, then I think there's definitely benefit for other, particularly remote, communities," Dr Harfield said.

" Local, community controlled health services understand their communities better than anyone else. "

title: Chemical manufacturer ends sales of controversial herbicide
text:
Major chemical manufacturer Syngenta is ending sales of the controversial herbicide paraquat in Australia, after the national regulator restricted its use.

Last month, the Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority (APVMA) introduced new limits and conditions on how the chemical can be used.

The APVMA found no evidence the chemical increased the risk of Parkinson's disease, if used safely with the authority's significant restrictions in place.

In a statement released on Friday, Syngenta ANZ said its decision to exit the paraquat market in Australia and New Zealand came after the APVMA's limit changes and its own commercial review.

"Regulatory constraints, combined with a highly complex and increasingly expensive supply chain, have made the paraquat herbicide products commercially unviable," managing director David Van Ryswyk said.

Paraquat is used to control weeds in a range of crops. (ABC Rural: Jess Davis)

'No longer sustainable'

In March, Syngenta announced plans to end production of paraquat at its UK plant, ceasing global production by the end of June.

At the time the company confirmed a commitment to supplying Australian farmers via a third-party manufacturer.

Now that's coming to an end as well.

"Dedicating significant resources to unprofitable legacy products is no longer sustainable," Mr Van Ryswyk said.

"Paraquat has been a highly valued productivity and conservation tool for many Australian and New Zealand growers.

"This decision, while difficult, allows us to redirect our resources," he said.

Uncertainty for farmers

Generic versions of the herbicide will continue to be sold in Australia, manufactured by other companies.

But Western Victorian farmer and Grain Producers Australia (GPA) spokesman Andrew Weidemann said Syngenta's exit created uncertainty.

"Syngenta has been the stable foundation of this market for decades," he said.

Mr Weidemann said there are many other paraquat chemicals available, but "unfortunately, most of them [are] coming out of China".

"[Syngenta's] withdrawal leaves some important questions about what happens next," he said.

Andrew Weidemann says Syngenta's exit from Australia creates uncertainty despite generic sales continuing. (ABC Wimmera: Gillian Aeria)

Mr Weidemann said he was concerned Syngenta's decision would make label changes required by the APVMA more difficult.

"Some of the changes in grams active and the withholding periods on late applications in crop, that work will fall clearly on the feet of the industry," he said.

"So it's going to be a cost and … that's going to be something that we as the industry will have to work through."

Syngenta said it would manage the phase-out of its paraquat products in strict alignment with the APVMA's designated sell-out and use-by timelines.

In a statement, the APVMA said it does not comment on the commercial decisions of individual companies.

title: Waratahs claim third straight Super Rugby Women's title
text:
We mentioned it the earlier post — the Waratahs peaked at the right time of the season.

They lost two regular-season matches to finish third on the standings but rose to the occasion when it counted, in the play-offs.

They were convincing 33-22 winners over the Western Force in the semifinals and carried that confidence into the season decider.

Waratahs skipper Emily Chancellor told ABC Sport earlier in the week her squad had tremendous self-belief, and that showed against the Drua.

The Waratahs were also rewarded for showing faith in a fresh halves pair, Tia Hinds and Waiaria Ellis.

They were a revelation in the semi and final, directing the Waratahs' attack with aplomb.

Perhaps a future Wallaroos halves combination?

Time will tell!

title: LeBron's new teammates go wild as NBA star announces move
text:
LeBron James's first "final" decision was that he would retire.

Weeks of deep reflection led him to change his mind, however, with all the familiar options in front of him to extend his career; a third trip with Cleveland, a second stop in Miami, maybe even stay in California for a high-profile union in Golden State.

But it was nope to all of those teams.

The blaring headline in bold letters still seemed like a feverish dream to the bulk of a fan base who was not even alive the last time the franchise won a title, but it is true: LeBron James is heading to the Philadelphia 76ers.

Loading Instagram content

The NBA's all-time leading scorer made the announcement on social media overnight, saying it will be his "last decision" and that it comes after he strongly considered retirement.

"I believe I can help make the Philadelphia 76ers a championship team and I am so excited to energise a new fan base and start this incredible journey one last time," James said.

A four-time NBA champion, James wrote he was "done" when his 23rd NBA season ended and that it was his last with the Los Angeles Lakers.

"I was pretty sure I played my last game. I was honest at that last press conference when I said I needed to look at myself and decide if I still love this game," James wrote.

"I still truly love this game, and I have more to give."

The 41-year-old James is set to sign a modest $US8 million ($11.4 million), two-year contract on the veteran minimum salary with the Sixers, according to ESPN. He made nearly $53 million last season.

"I'm not going for money. I'm not going for family," James wrote.

"What am I really playing for at this point? I still want to sacrifice. I still want to work. I still want to grind. I still want to compete, to win and to have a chance at the feeling of winning."

James celebrated his decision on Instagram with a career highlight reel set to Philadelphia rapper Meek Mill's Dreams and Nightmares, the adopted sports anthem of city teams.

LeBron James left the Los Angeles Lakers, with rumours connecting him to Miami, Cleveland, or another team in LA. (Getty Images: Harry How)

The video ends with the lyric, "hold up, wait a minute. Y'all thought I was finished?" and cuts to a 76ers' logo.

Sportswear company Fanatics already had his number 23 jersey on sale for $125 with delivery not expected until the end of August. The company sold out within hours of the announcement.

Much as James did for Cleveland when he ended a 56-year championship drought for the city by leading the Cavaliers to the title in 2016, he can snap a lengthy title drought for the Sixers.

The Sixers went 45-37 last season and were swept in the second round by the NBA champion New York Knicks.

Most betting sites had the Sixers as 9-1 favourites to win the championship behind the Oklahoma City Thunder, the San Antonio Spurs and the New York Knicks, as of Saturday morning.

James joins a 76ers team that has not won an NBA championship since 1983 and has not advanced out of the second round of the Eastern Conference play-offs since 2001.

Philadelphia star Tyrese Maxey reacts to the news LeBron James is joining the team. (Instagram: @tyresemaxey)

The 76ers should boast one of the top starting fives in the NBA with second-year standout VJ Edgecombe, fellow All-Stars Joel Embiid, Tyrese Maxey and Jaylen Brown — the 2024 NBA Finals MVP, a five-time All-Star and the league's fourth-leading scorer this past season acquired in a stunning off-season deal with the Celtics.

Maxey posted an Instagram story of him celebrating in a gym and yelling "What? What!" over the news while Brown wrote on X "#throwtheballup."

Brown wrote the same phrase in his introductory note to Philadelphia, and it has already been branded on billboards throughout the city.

Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro even proclaimed Friday as LeBron James Day in the state.

title: Businesses sue Trump as he defends 'very standard tariffs'
text:
Two small US businesses are suing Donald Trump to try to stop him from placing new tariffs on imports from scores of countries, including Australia.

The case has been taken up by non-profit law firm Liberty Justice Center, which successfully challenged Mr Trump's previous "liberation day" tariffs.

The new Trump tariffs, which include a 12.5 per cent levy on Australian imports, took effect on Friday.

The Trump administration imposed them after conducting trade investigations into all the US's major trading partners which found they were all doing too little to combat forced labour and slavery in supply chains.

The plaintiffs allege those findings were predetermined. Their legal complaint argues the new levies are instead designed to maintain a tariff regime that has already been deemed unlawful.

The complaint points out that Trump officials publicly stated, on multiple occasions, that they would find ways to bring back tariffs after Mr Trump's first attempt was struck down in court.

"Some of those statements were made before USTR [US Trade Representative] completed — or, in some cases, even began — the investigations supposedly supporting this new tariff regime," the Liberty Justice Center said.

'Forced labour' tariff rates 10 per cent: Argentina, Bangladesh, Cambodia, Canada, Ecuador, El Salvador, European Union, Guatemala, Honduras, India, Indonesia, Jordan, Malaysia, Mexico, Pakistan, Sri Lanka, Taiwan, Trinidad and Tobago, UK

Argentina, Bangladesh, Cambodia, Canada, Ecuador, El Salvador, European Union, Guatemala, Honduras, India, Indonesia, Jordan, Malaysia, Mexico, Pakistan, Sri Lanka, Taiwan, Trinidad and Tobago, UK 12.5 per cent: Algeria, Angola, Australia, the Bahamas, Bahrain, Brazil, Chile, China, Colombia, Costa Rica, Dominican Republic, Egypt, Guyana, Hong Kong, China, Iraq, Israel, Japan, Kazakhstan, Kuwait, Libya, Morocco, New Zealand, Nicaragua, Nigeria, Norway, Oman, Peru, the Philippines, Qatar, Russia, Saudi Arabia, Singapore, South Africa, South Korea, Switzerland, Thailand, Türkiye, UAE, Uruguay, Venezuela, Vietnam

Experts split on whether tariffs will survive

The Liberty Justice Center filed its lawsuit on behalf of spice importer Burlap & Barrel and watch-seller Collective Horology.

It was filed in the US Court of International Trade, which initially ruled Mr Trump's previous tariffs were invalid before the case went to the Supreme Court, which then endorsed the trade court's ruling.

Trump rebuilds his tariff wall Donald Trump had been using tariffs to increase his power over other countries until America's Supreme Court stepped in. He was never going to cede that power easily.

This latest lawsuit's prospects of success are unclear.

Some analysts say the new "Section 301" tariffs, named for the relevant part of trade law, are more likely to withstand a legal challenge.

Former US trade negotiator Wendy Cutler, who is now senior vice-president of the Asia Society Policy Institute, said: "The likelihood of courts overriding these tariffs is significantly lower than previous actions."

But Alan Wolff, a senior fellow at the Peterson Institute for International Economics, wrote the new tariffs "would represent another case of presidential overreach".

"If they were challenged in court, the Supreme Court would likely overturn them," said Mr Wolff, who has held senior trade positions with the US government and the World Trade Organization.

'Very standard tariffs', says Trump

Australian businesses say the new tariffs will make it harder to compete in the US and hurt Australian jobs.

The Australian government has also said it would argue "very forcefully" against the "unjustified" new tariffs.

But that effort will likely be limited to diplomatic negotiation rather than legal challenge.

Mr Trump today defended the new tariffs.

"They're very standard tariffs," he said.

"The other way was easier. I thought the decision by the Supreme Court was not a good one. But we have many forms of tariffs."

Before yesterday's decision, Australia's exports to the US had been subject to a 10 per cent tariff — initially under Mr Trump's "liberation day" regime, and later under a temporary measure that expired at the same time that the new tariff kicked in.

So Australia's tariff rate increased 2.5 percentage points when the tariff took effect on Friday.

title: Dog trainer says ABC's Muster Dogs is driving demand for working dogs
text:
Internationally renowned working dog trainer Gary White is in the business of training humans.

He travels Australia and the world, hosting workshops designed to help handlers get the most out of their working dog.

Participants bring their pup and test them in the yard, while White coaches them through training drills.

"It's more about teaching the handler where they've got to be and what they've got to do," White said.

"And when they know, they can actually teach their dog."

Gary White hosts working dog schools across Australia and overseas. (ABC Broken Hill: Kristina Rosengren)

White has lived on the land all of his life, and throughout that time he's always had a dog by his side.

While mustering increasingly involves the use of autogyros and drones, White is adamant that a good working dog will always have a place on a station.

In fact, he believes the ABC's hit series Muster Dogs is playing a part in a surge of demand for these canine employees.

It's a partnership

White grew up on a property between Nyngan and Cobar, in western New South Wales.

He spent most of that time working the land alone.

"My whole life I was virtually working by myself, with just me and the dogs. That's the way I loved it," White said.

"My dogs were my right-hand man."

A working dog can save a lot of physical work when mustering animals. (ABC Broken Hill: Kristina Rosengren)

His father, John White, started White's Kelpie Stud in the 1950s, a business which the younger White has continued.

Dog enthusiasts visiting the stud from America gave him the connection that eventually led to his first opportunity to host a training workshop in Iowa in 1999.

"It just all blossomed from there," White said.

"It's my life now, actually.

"I've been over to America and Canada eight times, all through Scandinavia and Europe."

Gary White has grown up with dogs all his life. (ABC Broken Hill: Kristina Rosengren)

The main focus of his lessons is the partnership between human and dog.

"I can pretty well pick straight away whether a dog suits an owner," White said.

"If we've got a dog that's very strong-headed, and doesn't want the partnership to blossom with the human, and doesn't work so much with the human, it can be hard work."

Worth every penny

A report released by ANZ last year found that the demand for working dogs had increased over the past decade, particularly given the strain on the agricultural workforce.

It's a story White is not unfamiliar with.

"When I was contracting, they'd employ me with my team of working dogs instead of employing another two people," White said.

"They're very cost-effective."

The highest price paid at a recent dog auction was almost $30,000. (ABC Broken Hill: Kristina Rosengren)

White said while they're worth the money, the average price for working dogs has been steadily rising.

At a dog auction in Forbes in mid-July, the highest price paid for a dog was $28,500.

"There's a lot of dogs being sold from between $20,000 and $30,000 these days," White said.

"[Some] dogs are selling up to $50,000."

While there were many factors contributing to the high price, White said goats had something to do with it.

"It has traditionally been the goat market that has pushed the price of dogs," he said.

Gary White says high prices for goats have pushed up the price for working dogs. (ABC Landline: Tony Hill)

"The price of dogs [has jumped] over the years by people catching goats because people could see … the dollar value.

"If [someone] pays $10,000 for a dog, and they go out and muster in that first week $10,000 worth of goats, that's a cheap dog."

While they may be hardy workers, White believes the value of a dog goes beyond rounding up sheep and cattle.

For many working in agriculture, they're also a companion during arduous, long days and trying times.

A working dog is more than just an employee, for many they're also a much-loved mate. (ABC Broken Hill: Kristina Rosengren)

"Some people just love their dogs to bits, and they're widely called their best mate," White said.

"Their dogs [have] helped them get through sticky situations.

"I know people that [say] their dogs actually helped them through the drought."

Always a place for a working dog

For more than six decades, John Lawrence of Nine Mile Station has had at least a couple of working dogs.

"You must have dogs," Lawrence said.

"We've got pretty hard country, like hilly country, and it's pretty difficult to get around sheep at times.

"The dog jumps off, and he's got them together in no time flat and saves you trying to bounce away up and down over rocks and hills."

John Lawrence has never gone without working dogs on the station. (ABC Broken Hill: Kristina Rosengren)

Over the years, Lawrence has seen technology evolve to the point where motorbikes, autogyros and drones have become a necessity to cover the vast lands of the outback.

"From horses to planes and drones," Lawrence said.

"The motorbikes are so much better now than what they used to be when we first started."

But despite the vast improvements, Lawrence said there will always be a place for dogs in mustering.

"I think young people are realising how important it is to have dogs," he said.

"That's why I see so many turn up to these schools, because people are using dogs a lot more than what they did."

Ruger and Cash are never far away from their owner, Peter Leigo, on Netley Station. (ABC Broken Hill: Kristina Rosengren)

Peter Leigo is a station hand at Netley Station, south of Broken Hill.

title: Quick hits: Aussie's dash to glory, Englishman drops his lollies
text:
A broken lane rope holds up the swimming program, an Australian wins gold after a mad dash from the medal podium and an Englishman drops his lollies.

Here are the quick hits from day one of the Commonwealth Games.

1. Broken lane rope

A broken lane rope delayed a heat of the men's 100m breaststroke. (Getty Images: PA Images/Owen Humphreys)

There is a whole host of things you probably do not want to see when you are about to dive into the pool ahead of a major championship.

One of them faced Zac Stubblety-Cook ahead of the 100-metre breaststroke heat, when he saw the lane rope had popped out of its holder.

"I was a bit worried, and nobody noticed. It was in my lane," Stubblety-Cook told the Seven Network.

Stubblety-Cook backed away from his block and alerted the authorities, who initially seemed to make things worse, with part of the rope falling into the pool as an official precariously reached for it pool side.

His attempts were unsuccessful at first, as the swimmers sat back down for what felt like an indeterminable wait (ultimately about 15 minutes).

"I've never had a delay that long," Stubblety-Cook said.

"That's just sport. You have to roll with it."

Easily done, perhaps, for a 27-year-old four-time Olympic medallist and former world champion, but what about if you are 23-years-old and making your major championship debut?

"I think it's expected to expect the unexpected," Bailey Lello said.

Well said young man, and well swam too. He made it to the semifinals alongside Stubblety-Cook and Sam Williamson.

2. All in a day's (or hour's) work

Jenna Forrester shows off her gold medal after winning the women's 200m backstroke final. (Getty Images: Michael Steele)

In the space of an hour, Australia's Jenna Forrester mastered multi-tasking.

After finishing third behind fellow Australian Lani Pallister in the women's 400m freestyle final, Forrester took part in the medal ceremony and the photo opportunities that come with that ritual.

She then raced to the call room, needing to back up for the women's 200m backstroke final.

Forrester could be forgiven if she was out of breath but managed to win gold in astonishing fashion.

What made her victory even more remarkable was the fact she initially missed qualifying for the event after placing fourth at last month's selection trials in Sydney.

She only got a berth in the 200m backstroke when Australia's backstroke great Kaylee McKeown withdrew from the Games with glandular fever.

"I don't know what to say and didn't expect it to happen," Forrester told the Seven Network.

"I gave it my all and I'm so proud of myself. I am shocked."

3. Englishman drops his lollies

The pause button was hit on Australia's clash with England in the men's 3x3 wheelchair basketball competition for an unusual reason: one of the England players dropped his lollies.

Play was halted after lollies fell from the pocket of England captain Peter Cusack.

Officials asked staff for some assistance clearing the court surface, but Cusack waved them away.

He politely scooped up the fallen cargo and took them to the side of court before re-joining the game.

4. Sister rivalry either side of Hadrian's wall

Astrid Carroll (left) represents Scotland, while younger sister Ursula Carroll represents England. (Getty Images)

The single heat of the women's 100m S13 freestyle event had something of an unusual quirk in it.

Teenage sisters Ursula and Astrid Carroll were both making their international debuts, but for different countries.

The reason is not quite as spicy as one might hope, even with the countries at stake being Auld Enemies England and Scotland.

Astrid, 17, was born in Edinburgh, so she swims for Scotland, while her 14-year-old sister Ursula was born in Halifax, the people's republic of Yorkshire, so she swims for England.

The pair both live with Stargardt disease, a rare, inherited eye condition that causes progressive, central vision loss, "basically like seeing through a doughnut" Astrid told the BBC.

"It'll be nice walking out and just seeing you," Astrid added in that same interview.

Ursula simply responded the only way she could have, as an Englishwoman: "Scottish, unbelievable."

In the heats, Ursula got the win over her big sister, swimming 1:05.25 to Astrid's 1:05.84.

5. It's all in a name

De Niro Pao (right) took on Pooana Khoahli in the men's 65kg class. (Getty Images: Lintao Zhang)

Did Niue's De Niro Pao chose boxing or did boxing choose De Niro Pao?

If you are wondering where we are going here, let's hear from Pao himself.

"Robert De Niro is my mum's favourite actor, so she named me after him," Pao said.

"That's my grandad's favourite actor too."

Of course, De Niro won an Oscar for his portrayal of boxer Jake LaMotta in the 1980 film Raging Bull.

Given Pao competed in the men's boxing in Glasgow, perhaps he psyched himself up with a viewing of Martin Scorsese's classic?

Perhaps not.

"My grandad always tells me about Raging Bull, but I've never seen it," Pao admits.

For the record, Pao was eliminated via a points decision in the men's 65kg class, going down to Lesotho's Pooana Khoahli.

title: Fifteen minutes after celebrating bronze, Forrester stuns with gold
text:
Jenna Forrester wasn't even supposed to be there.

The 23-year-old travelled to Glasgow as a 400m freestyle and individual medley swimmer.

Then, when backstroke queen Kaylee McKeown succumbed to illness on the eve of the Commonwealth Games, selectors decided to throw Forrester in the 200m back too.

Such is the depth in Australian swimming, that's usually a pretty solid tactic to nab a podium double or even the vaunted sweep.

But usually it's not the afterthought climbing the top step.

"I really just went into tonight with a positive attitude," she said.

Swimmers spark medal rush on day one Lani Pallister wins Australia's first gold of these Commonwealth Games in the women's 400m freestyle, with more Aussies scooping up medals in the pool on the first full day of competition.

"I felt like I had nothing to lose and my family would have been really proud of me no matter what the result was. I feel like I really just took that in my stride."

At the trials in June, it was 20-year-old Iona Anderson who announced herself as a potential heir to McKeown's throne when she bettered her qualifying time.

McKeown, in the depths of glandular fever, responded in the final with a dominant victory, besting Anderson by almost four seconds in the final.

Hannah Fredericks was third and Forrester was more than five seconds behind McKeown in fourth.

For much of Saturday morning's final, it appeared something similar would repeat, albeit without the knowledge that everyone is racing for silver behind McKeown.

Fredericks was out fastest, while Forrester sat sixth at the first turn.

In fact, Fredericks led for the first three quarters of the race, before slowing in the last lap with only a 34-second split of the top six.

Meanwhile, Forrester was only getting stronger, saving her second-fastest 50 metres for last as she mowed down her compatriot, Scotland's Katie Shanahan, and Canadian Madison Kryger.

Forrester was a surprise gold medallist on night one. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

A veteran of three world championships, a Commonwealth Games and an Olympics before arriving in Glasgow, this marks her first gold medal at a major meet.

The stamina on display was remarkable for a woman who, only 15 minutes earlier, was standing on the podium celebrating her 400m freestyle bronze alongside champion teammate Lani Pallister.

Exactly how she managed to pull that off remains a mystery even to her.

"I honestly couldn't tell you, I am as shocked as you are," she said.

"I think my training this year has been really consistent and I have all of Swimming Australia and my coaches to thank for that.

"Honestly, I couldn't have done it without the help of a lot of others."

And on a night when 15 of her fellow Dolphins also won medals, there's plenty of help around.

title: Pogačar claims stunning victory in stage 19 of the Tour de France
text:
Tadej Pogačar launched a stunning solo attack from the foot of the iconic Alpe d'Huez to win the 19th stage of the Tour de France and extend his overall lead overnight.

Even by the four-time Tour champion's lofty standards, it was up there with his best wins as he was more than 3 minutes behind with 12km remaining.

Riding without a teammate for the last section, he caught Ecuadorian rider Richard Carapaz and Frenchman Lenny Martinez with 1.5km left and then surged ahead for his fifth stage win of this year's race and 26th overall.

"It's very cool to win up here," Pogačar said. "I'm super happy to take the win."

Martinez finished six seconds behind and Carapaz — who won the 18th stage with a brilliant breakaway win of his own — nine seconds back. American Sepp Kuss, who faded in the closing stages, was 1 minute, 14 seconds adrift.

With a lead of 7 minutes, 11 seconds over Remco Evenepoel in the overall standings, and two stages remaining, Pogačar is on the brink of joining Eddy Merckx, Miguel Indurain, Jacques Anquetil and Bernard Hinault as the only men to win five Tours.

Barring mishap or accident, the Slovenian star will be crowned when the race ends on Sunday on the Champs-Élysées in Paris.

Rated as an HC mountain pass, the hardest category in the race, Alpe d'Huez is arguably the most famed climb in cycling and has near-mythical status on the Tour. Swarms of fans, many camping overnight and carrying flags of several nations, screamed encouragement on each of the 21 hairpins.

"It was a crazy atmosphere on the whole climb," Pogačar said.

He kept his focus as the public got perilously close to his face and, at one stage, he had limited visibility due to smoke from flares being lit by spectators.

But as impressive as Pogačar's win was, it also came about because Carapaz, Kuss and Martinez did not work together properly to distance Pogačar when he was lower down.

"I had to fight against super good riders," Pogačar said. "But they were playing against each other a bit so it helped me to catch up."

Perhaps thinking he could benefit from others fading and get the stage win, Martinez kept sitting on Carapaz's wheel, which was very much to Carapaz's annoyance and meant the veteran had too much work to do alone.

He kept trying to accelerate while Martinez — 10 years his junior — did less work and a tired-looking Kuss generally sat back too much before drifting away.

With 900m left, Carapaz was showing phenomenal stamina to stay with Pogačar, but he was finally undone by a brutal acceleration and could not follow as the yellow jersey rolled past him.

Saturday's mammoth 171m Alpine stage could be epic.

It features three HC climbs — Col de la Croix de Fer, Col du Galibier and Col de Sarenne — and one Category 1 climb up Col du Télégraphe before a hilly finish to Alpe d'Huez.

Pogačar does not need to go for victory and can safely hang back and protect his lead.

But will he?

There are 66m of pure climbing, and that may be too much for him to resist.

"Tomorrow is the Queen stage of the Tour," Pogačar said. "[It] is the hardest day of the Tour. We'll follow our own plan, our own rhythm. We don't care about anything else."

“I’m gonna buy a saxophone.” The tone in my gig buddy’s voice was part “damn the torpedoes” and part “tell Laura I love her”. He knew the risks. This was incendiary stuff for a professional rock musician so he said it discreetly, as Paul Von Mertens from the Pet Sounds Band expertly rearranged the oxygen in the hall. The sight of a saxophone hero at the lip of the pop stage is a rare thing these days. It’s why Doja Cat exhuming Kenny G caused such a splash at last year’s VMA Awards. It’s how Bernard Fanning and Paul Dempsey sealed their bold departure from alt-rock expectations on their super album, The Deluge. Somewhere around grunge o’clock, the saxophone roared off a cliff in a cream linen suit. But it’s coming back. AP This long after Baker Street and Careless Whisper, the sax doesn’t beckon – it dares. Music researchers John Laughter and Steve D. Marshall have documented its popular profile across the decades in stark numbers. A Cornell University study later crunched them to identify two golden ages for the instrument, both long ago. Most spectacularly, from 1958 to 1962, an average of 55 Top-40 hits a year contained a saxophone solo. This timeframe doesn’t even count the classic rock ‘n’ roll era of Rock Around the Clock, Tutti Frutti, Long Tall Sally et al, when the rude honk seemed as foundational as guitars and drums.

Advertisement

The lesser golden age, from 1978 to 1982, was still blessed with an average of 27 Top-40 sax solos per year. And this was before MTV started steaming up our windows with Let’s Dance, True, The Heat Is On, Smooth Operator, Danger Zone, Out of Mind, Out of Sight and Never Tear Us Apart. Bruce Springsteen, with saxophonist Clarence Clemons, knows the value of a good sax solo. AP Then came the long exhale. By 1998 to 2002, the average had fallen to less than one a year, where it more or less remains today. The evidence is clear. Somewhere around grunge o’clock, the saxophone didn’t so much sashay into the sunset as roar off a cliff in a cream linen suit. Why? Pop used to wield Adolphe Sax’s steampunk contraption like Arthur brandished Excalibur. Remember oiled colossus Tim Cappello pumping his sax like iron in The Lost Boys? Springsteen basking in Clarence Clemons’ mojo on the cover of Born to Run? Bowie only played his sometimes, but he sure knew how to hold one in a promo shot.

Advertisement

Even Kenny G is acceptable again. NBCUniversal via Getty Images This propensity for pulling focus may be part of the problem. It’s “too much of a main character to remain always in a supporting role”, I’m told by one Melbourne saxophonist who requested anonymity to speak freely. He also wonders if its lung-powered timbre might place it too close in the mix to the human voice, “and let’s face it, lead singers are not inclined to stand aside”. It would explain how the sax has retained its dignity in the jazz scene, where singers tend to know their place further down the pecking order. In the all-about-me world of the modern singer-songwriter, even guitarists have learnt to keep their dirty boots off the monitors. “The saxophone is perfectly suited to a horn section, the problem is, most sax players aren’t,” my source opines. Ultimately, they’re “frustrated they can’t show everyone how awesome the sax is at taking the lead all of the time”. In a nostalgic context, that awesomeness remains undeniable. Nobody who leaves an Icehouse show these days soon forgets the one-man cavalry of Hugo Lee, swaggering from the back of the stage to the brink of the pit to raise his horn like a Viking chugging the blood of a freshly slain ram.

Advertisement

In coming months, Colin Hay’s reconstituted Men at Work will honour the legacy of the great Greg Ham with the monster sax riffs of Who Can It Be Now? and Overkill. The Dire Straits Experience, led not by some guitar player but by the band’s former saxophonist, Chris White, will surely find plenty of reasons to moisten the reed. Related Article Opinion

The Verdict Looking for an antidote to the attention economy? Stop scrolling and try this Paul Kalina Editor, Green Guide and The Guide There’s hope brewing in the present, too. Sax cameos rolled out by Doja Cat and The Weeknd feel more like dalliances than bold-as-brass conviction. But the Viagra Boys, Radio Free Alice, dust and O. are among those clawing back righteous ground. Sydney drums/sax duo Party Dozen has blown minds opening for Amyl and the Sniffers in Europe and North America. Still, we’re a long way from Baker Street. After decades of tasteful textures and emotional half-light filtered through sad singers’ navel lint, that rip-snorting blast of hot air is exactly the voice pop needs to rediscover: a brash, sweaty beast wearing sunglasses indoors that says, “Stand back sweethearts, I’m taking this one home.” “The fingering is basically the same as the flute,” my intrepid gig buddy added in my ear that night. Crazy talk, obviously. But once we get the saxophone back in charge, anything might be possible. Get a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own. title: ‘It dispelled a bunch of shame’: How a writing group is helping locals share revealing true stories
text:
Advertisement

CultureTheatreArt ‘It dispelled a bunch of shame’: How a writing group is helping locals share revealing true stories Garry Maddox July 25, 2026 — 11:40am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

When Cas Castellano moved to Australia from Philadelphia, she found it hard to fit in with her new community. That changed when she found a writing group, wrote a story about a dark time in her life and read it aloud on stage. “It’s a story that’s true but not necessarily one I’d brag about on the street,” she says. “It’s been amazing watching the community get to know each other and remember that most people are carrying a sadness they don’t want to reveal”: Rob Carlton and Adrienne Ferreira James Brickwood Castellano, 30, found it was liberating reading that story – about binge-drinking, cutting herself and breaking into buildings with a boyfriend as she struggled with her father’s declining mental health – in front of 200 people at a live performance night. “It dispelled a bunch of shame that I was carrying,” she says. “The reaction was overwhelmingly positive. It meant something to them but they weren’t judging me for it.”

Advertisement

Advertisement

“She felt like her family was failing, that she had to hide the truth from the world, that she was running away,” he says. “All she was feeling was the negative elements of it. All the audience could see was a young woman trying to manage a really difficult situation.” At a time when loneliness and isolation are all too common – away from busier entertainment areas in Sydney and Newcastle – Carlton says Bravewords Live sells out every month. “It’s the community every time going, ‘that’s me up on stage’,” he says. “It’s been amazing watching [them] get to know each other and remember that most people are carrying a sadness they don’t want to reveal.” Along the way, Bravewords has helped rejuvenate the struggling central business district in Gosford. Ferreira says she has seen lives transformed by learning to tell a personal tale - their motto is “true stories well told” - then sharing it on stage. The format of reading it means there’s no pressure to memorise or perform.

Advertisement

Some participants have discovered a talent for writing and have found like-minded friends for future projects. Audience members have bonded by sharing their own versions of the night’s stories over a meal after the show. While it sounds like therapy, Ferreira is reluctant to call it that “only because that’s not the intention from the get-go. But this is what art does, right? It’s therapeutic and it’s cathartic and it connects”. Related Article Performing arts As the world burns, we all want to get a little weird Carlton discovered the format at Story Club, the long-running live comedy show founded by Zoe Norton Lodge and Ben Jenkins in inner Sydney that was briefly an ABC series in 2015. (With Jenkins moving on to create the Stan series The Killings at Parrish Station, Osher Gunsberg has taken over hosting with Norton Lodge) Taking part, Carlton learnt that by adding drama, humanity and vulnerability to a story rather than going for quick laughs, “you get a bigger laugh at the end of it and you also get a deeper connection to the struggle of what it is to be alive”.

Advertisement

He saw the value of these stories when a mental health nurse hired him to speak to farmers going through a drought in the Narrabri Shire, north-west of Tamworth, in 2020. He combined some of his stories into a show directed by comic Darren Gilshenan. “The year before they ran suicide awareness workshops and not one farmer turned up because they called them that,” Carlton says. “Then they had this great idea to call it What a Relief: It’s Rob Carlton. We went out with a financial planning person and a mental health nurse. We were just masquerading, but it was really a mental health initiative.” “The reaction was overwhelmingly positive”: Cas Castellano tells a personal story at Bravewords Live on the NSW Central Coast. Bravewords It worked, as a way for the nurse to start conversations with farmers about their struggles. Carlton combined four of his own stories from Bravewords Live into the hit one-man show Virgin in a Knife Fight that, after debuting in Gosford in January, has run at fringe and comedy festivals in Perth, Adelaide, Newcastle, Canberra, Melbourne and Sydney. It runs at Glen Street Theatre in northern Sydney next month.

Advertisement

As well as being funny and heartfelt, Carlton’s show has a serious intention as it interweaves stories from his life. “My goal is to encourage conversations across the generations,” he says. Lifeline 13 11 14 Virgin In A Knife Fight is at Glen Street Theatre, Belrose, on August 21-22. The next Bravewords Live is at Funhaus Factory, Gosford, on August 30. title: A generation lost? The risky game played by our Test selectors
text:
Advertisement

SportCricketAustralian cricket Opinion A generation lost? The risky game played by our Test selectors Daniel Brettig The Age chief cricket writer Updated July 25, 2026 — 11:30am , first published July 25, 2026 — 7:00am

Updated July 25, 2026 — 11:30am ,first published July 25, 2026 — 7:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

“Old blokes win stuff” was a phrase beloved of all-rounder and now coach Dan Christian, as he spent his final few playing years hoovering up Twenty20 franchise trophies around the world. It’s also a neat summary of the philosophy followed by the national selectors, as they do all they can to keep the ageing core of the Australian Test team together for a glut of major assignments over the next 12 months. Still together after all these years: Australian bowlers Josh Hazlewood, Nathan Lyon, Mitchell Starc and Pat Cummins in 2018. AP When selection chair George Bailey, coach Andrew McDonald and selector Tony Dodemaide got together in 2022, they agreed on an approach that marked a significant departure from previous panels. Rather than playing their best team whenever possible, the focus was narrowed to major events. Test series and World Cups were king, while bilateral white-ball series fell a long way down the order of preference. They have effectively become proving grounds for young players, as well as contractual obligations for Cricket Australia.

Advertisement

The Test match focus on the now was enhanced by the aim of securing a spot in the world championship final every two years, adding context to lower-profile series dotted in between bouts against England and India. By rationing resources, they hoped to extend the careers of great players. Editor's pick Australian cricket Final frontier: Smith and ageing Test team vow to complete unfinished business away from home Four years on, however, a two-match series against Bangladesh in Darwin and Mackay seems an odd juncture at which to roll out Steve Smith, Josh Hazlewood, Mitchell Starc, Scott Boland and Nathan Lyon, all of whom are now 35 and older. There are sensible arguments for reconvening the frontline Test team ahead of 12 unrelenting months of series against South Africa, New Zealand, India and England. But the prospect of playing an XI with only one player under the age of 30, against a Bangladesh side that just lost a Test by an innings to Zimbabwe, is an unsettling one. The flipside of Australia’s approach over the past four years has been that opportunities for younger players are only provided when there is an injury or an obvious gap in the side.

Advertisement

That has meant the likes of Sam Konstas, Nathan McSweeney and Todd Murphy have been exposed to Test cricket in the toughest circumstances: against a rampaging Jasprit Bumrah, in the crucible of an Ashes series in England, or on uneven Caribbean pitches against Shamar Joseph. Those experiences were bruising ones for the trio, more so for being followed by omission from the team. It would have been useful to see any one of these players granted the opportunity to impose themselves on Bangladesh. After all, a Travis Head blitz is not going to prove much the selectors don’t already know, nor will a brace of hundreds by Smith do much more than pad out his formidable Test record. Numerous senior figures in the game spoken to by this masthead expressed surprise at the absence of even one young batter from the squad. Konstas and Ollie Peake were both mentioned by several as ideal candidates to play. The 13 chosen this week will likely be augmented by other non-playing squad members around the two Tests, but their exposure will be limited to training sessions. Jasprit Bumrah gets Nathan McSweeney for a duck in Perth in 2024. Getty Images As it is, Jake Weatherald, Cameron Green and Marnus Labuschagne will be the trio most eager to find runs and confidence in Darwin and Mackay, having offered only glimpses of their best in last summer’s Ashes series. Weatherald’s chemistry with Head is obvious, but Test cricket is a game of performance rather than a rom com.

Advertisement

A more persuasive argument for playing an old team against Bangladesh comes in the form of using the series as a quasi-fitness test. Hazlewood, Cummins and Lyon in particular need to reassure the selectors of their ability to stay on the park, making the Top-End Tests a useful juncture to do so before the South Africa tour. While Cummins’ back stress injury may ultimately work in favour of longevity, meaning he has more Test matches to play over the next three years or so, Hazlewood and Lyon are facing stiffer questions of durability. Editor's pick Australian cricket Why Australia’s next Test opponents are in crisis mode Hazlewood has now pulled up lame in his first long-form game back from injury too many times for comfort, while Lyon’s soft-tissue problems should at the very least necessitate he is moved away from outfield duty and remoulded, Jimmy Anderson style, into a close catcher. In the meantime, CA have an invitational XI going north to play Bangladesh in their warm-up fixture. Another group is heading to Chennai for the annual visit to the MRF Academy in India. Australia A tour India later in the year. Numerous white ball players may travel there, rather than playing in concurrent limited overs series against South Africa and Zimbabwe.

Advertisement

Apart from Konstas, Peake, Cooper Connolly and Campbell Kellaway, Australia also have an emerging generation of fast bowlers currently navigating the same kinds of injuries once traversed by Cummins and company. In years to come, the likes of Callum Vidler and Mahli Beardman will get the chance to make their mark. There is still hope for Lance Morris and Jhye Richardson, too. For now, the selectors continue to err on the side of experience, even for an opponent as modest as Bangladesh. History will be the judge of whether they have pulled the right rein. title: Odysseus didn’t rest on his laurels. But like the rest of us, maybe he should have
text:
Advertisement

LifestyleLife & relationshipsWork/life balance Opinion Odysseus didn’t rest on his laurels. But like the rest of us, maybe he should have Julia Baird Journalist, broadcaster, historian and author July 25, 2026 — 9:30am

July 25, 2026 — 9:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The phrase “resting on your laurels” hasn’t always been a criticism; once it was a point of praise. Instead of suggesting complacency and laziness, it was a public recognition of achievement. In Ancient Greece, athletes were awarded wreaths of laurel leaves – also known as bay leaves, the kind you pop into a soup or stock. The term had arisen from mythology and the age-old phenomenon of spurned men really not picking up the vibe. In short, the god Apollo had the hots for the beautiful river nymph Daphne, and pursued her doggedly despite her lack of interest. One day, when he was chasing her and had just caught her, she begged her father, the river god, to save her. Naturally, he turned her into a laurel tree. (To be fair, Cupid, annoyed with Apollo, had shot him with a gold-tipped arrow of love and Daphne with a lead-tipped arrow of repulsion, so this was never going to go well.) Matt Damon as Odysseus and Zendaya as Athena in The Odyssey. Apollo tried to salvage this turn of events by kissing the tree, whispering: “Since you cannot be my bride, you must be my tree!” He hacked off some branches to make a wreath for his head. Laurels became crowns of victory. From the 6th century BC, bay leaves were placed on the head of every winner at the Pythian Games in Delphi. Now, with the broad public dissection of The Odyssey, a rare box-office triumph, including talk of Odysseus’ relentless drive, I’d like to suggest we revert to the original, Grecian meaning of this long-misused term. Tell people to rest on their laurels for a bit! Stick it to the “rise and grind” of hustle culture, and celebrate a time to pause, regroup, be satisfied after something you’ve accomplished, instead of maniacally thundering towards the next hurdle.

Advertisement

When Chaucer wrote The Knight’s Tale in the late 1300s, he wrote that when someone is crowned with laurels, he is “crowned a conqueror [who] lived in joy and honour”. This, in my view, is what the phrase should mean: joy and honour. You’ve achieved something? Rest up, relax, marinate in that joy and honour. Related Article Cinema Confused by the gods, monsters and mortals of The Odyssey? This is your cheat sheet Then, as with so many traditions, things took a dark turn in Regency and Victorian times. In 1825, The Literary Chronicle and Weekly Review told novelist Maria Edgeworth that despite her literary success, she must not rest: “We do not affect to wish she should repose on her laurels and rest satisfied; on the contrary, we believe that genius is inexhaustible … For Miss Edgeworth there must be no rest on this side the grave.” This is so daft. As though it’s a bad thing to “rest satisfied”. The fact that the meaning of laurel-resting has flipped so firmly since its inception is surely a sign of the ushering-in of hustle culture following both the industrial and technological revolutions. (Note that the hustle is always assumed to occur in jobs outside the home, despite the considerable hustle within.) And anyway, why is Odysseus, a man who left his wife and son for decades to carry on in other countries, now being heralded simply as a hero without the observation that he is also the central figure in a cautionary tale?

Advertisement

Ryan Holiday, a bestselling author and advocate for stoicism, says that those who find Odysseus inspiring miss the fact that when he arrives home after a 20-year journey, he quickly turns on his heels and goes out raiding in an attempt to build wealth. He is restless, unsated, discontent. Related Article Cinema 17 kilometres of film, $47 a ticket: How The Odyssey is resurrecting film Holiday cites a poem I was obsessed with as a teenager, and stuffed into my backpack when I travelled: Ulysses by Tennyson. (Read it here.) The old king is pondering his life and future, his unquiet soul and inability to stop wandering the earth: “I cannot rest from travel: I will drink/Life to the lees … always roaming with a hungry heart”. He continues: “I am a part of all that I have met;/Yet all experience is an arch wherethro’/Gleams that untravell’d world whose margin fades/For ever and forever when I move./How dull it is to pause …” When I was a teenager, stomping around Europe with backpack and boots, this hunger for adventure mirrored my own. But now I can better see that perhaps the man needed to relax for a bit, spend time with his wife and son. Stoics generally recognised Odysseus’ good qualities, such as a capacity to endure and resist temptation. However, as Holiday points out, Stoics like Seneca objected to the romanticising of Odysseus and considered his insatiable appetites for motion more curse than blessing. Sometimes we forget the beauty of the pause, especially after a period of struggle. In the same way we tell people to “move on”, to rush past relationships or grief or the pain of giving birth, we need to have words and respect for a period when a kite lands, having sliced through clouds. To stop, to look in wonder. This doesn’t mean never trying again, not working hard in the future – nor sitting around gloating – just that, for a period, you should allow yourself to be content without punishing yourself with the next goal, or measuring your distance from various heights that others may have reached.

Advertisement

Surely we can accept that exhaustion does not equate to accomplishment? The automatic response to “how have you been?” shouldn’t be “yeah, crazy-busy, hectic, flat out”. Related Article Opinion

Film Hey Elon Musk, The Odyssey doesn’t fail because it’s woke. It’s not woke enough Bill Wyman Contributor As Angie Dixon wrote in digital magazine OnlySky after being forced into retirement by disability: “The reward for productivity is the expectation of more productivity. You finish one project and receive another. You hit one goal and create a bigger one. There is no finish line. Nobody appears with a certificate declaring that you have finally done enough and may now rest without guilt.” Well, if you’d like a certificate, please accept this column as one. Pin a bay leaf in your hair, or slip it into your wallet as a reminder that you’ve worked hard, you’ve cared immensely and that, when the time is right, you really should go and have some sweet rest on those laurels. Julia Baird is a journalist, author and regular columnist. Her latest book is Bright Shining: how grace changes everything. title: New blow for LIV Golf as Asian Tour partners with rivals
text:
Advertisement

SportGolfLIV Golf Series New blow for LIV Golf as Asian Tour partners with rivals Evin Priest July 25, 2026 — 9:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Professional golf’s four-year turf war appears close to being over after LIV Golf was dealt hammer blows by America’s PGA Tour and the DP World Tour this week as the rebel league’s tournament was being held in the Midlands of England. LIV was already reeling from the withdrawal of financier Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund, but now the hopes it can continue into 2027 have taken a fresh hit. LIV Golf star Cameron Smith. Getty Images On Tuesday, while LIV golfers were playing practice rounds at the JCB course in England, news broke that the Asian Tour was partnering with LIV’s rivals, the DP World Tour and the PGA Tour. A new three-tour partnership will see pathways created for players from Asia to the top two levels in Europe, as well as co-sanctioned tournaments. While LIV is in the market seeking investment for 2027, it was a significant hurdle to jump because the Asian Tour had been a vital stepping stone to LIV.

Advertisement

Originally, the Asian Tour had aligned with LIV in a $US300 million partnership ahead of its 2022 launch, and in turn created the cashed-up “International Series”, which LIV golfers frequently played in. As a feeder tour, the International Series had also been vital to the promotion and relegation aspect of LIV – its 2026 season featured the top two players from the series’ order of merit list. As a secondary circuit, the Asian Tour also helped provide LIV with an external pathway for player turnover – an issue that had long been scrutinised during the league’s original pursuit of Official World Golf Ranking recognition. LIV can still stage its own qualifying school, but building a credible promotion pathway without the Asian Tour now becomes considerably more complex. The Asian Tour was also important because some of its historic national opens were part of LIV’s future plans.

Advertisement

With LIV’s future under a cloud, Asian Tour chief executive Cho Minn Thant said he had to consider pathways for his member players. “I think the timing is just right now; it’s all about timing,” Thant said this week. “We’d kept in touch [with the DP World Tour] over all these years. [In 2022], it was right for us to do a partnership with LIV Golf, but given the circumstances now, we’ve had to look at other options. Pathways to different tours are very important for our members.” Cho Minn Thant with LIV Golf’s Greg Norman in 2022. Getty Images After the Asian Tour news, the obstacles mounted for LIV. A report surfaced on Wednesday quoting two-time major winner Martin Kaymer, who captains the Cleeks GC team on LIV, saying that it was “highly unlikely” the $US40 million Team Championships finale in Michigan would go ahead. Then, on Thursday, the popular social media account Flushing It Golf – which has cultivated considerable access to tour players – published a post after speaking to a host of players at the JCB course.

Advertisement

Flushing It detailed how seven players told the account they plan to exit LIV after the 2026 season, “regardless of whether LIV Golf finds funding”. A clear pathway back to the PGA Tour was forged this year by former LIV golfers, American Patrick Reed and Eugenio Chacarra from Spain, who departed the league for the DP World Tour. American golfer Patrick Reed. Getty Images Reed and Chacarra, who have won multiple times on the DP World Tour this year, are ranked within the top three on its points list and are in line to receive two of the 10 cards on the PGA Tour for 2027 awarded to Europe’s best season-long points earners. This was followed by revelations that the volume of players from LIV seeking assurances from the DP World Tour about individual playing opportunities for 2027 had increased “significantly” in the past few weeks.

Advertisement

LIV has two more individual tournaments after England, including stops in New Jersey and Indianapolis. Related Article British Open ‘All hell broke loose’: Herbert reveals toll of LIV Golf uncertainty, says he considered quitting Sports fans now watch on to see what the future holds for a league that was reported to have received $US5 billion from the PIF since its creation in 2022. LIV disrupted the entire ecosystem of professional golf, luring massive stars such as Bryson DeChambeau, Australia’s own Cameron Smith, Dustin Johnson, Jon Rahm and others. The league’s enormous tournament purses and guaranteed roster forced the PGA Tour to keep up via supercharging prizemoney. There were positive outcomes for fans, including LIV pushing the PGA Tour to streamline its competition structure to entice top players to compete together more often and develop a more innovative TV broadcast. Australia also benefited in receiving the world-class LIV Adelaide tournament. But ultimately, a league that initially promised “golf, but louder” is struggling to be heard. The next few months will determine whether LIV Golf survives, is radically reinvented, or quietly fades away.

title: Despite everything FIFA threw at it, football really was the winner
text:
Advertisement

SportSoccerFIFA World Cup Opinion Despite everything FIFA threw at it, football really was the winner Malcolm Knox Journalist, author and columnist July 25, 2026 — 9:30am

July 25, 2026 — 9:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

“So it’s over – the few weeks every four years when you pretend you know something about football.” Cutting words to hear, at the end of an all-absorbing FIFA World Cup. My son spoke with his hand over his mouth, so I appealed to the referee (his mother) to get him sent off, but she was busy watching video replays. Soccer unites the world in sore-loserism. Illustration: Letch Having lost the point, I went down screaming in agony, ankle in one hand, eye socket in the other, rolling downhill on a flat floor. This earnt a red card for “blatant simulation”, so I called the President of the United States to get it overturned. But he was busy taking a call from Bryson DeChambeau whining at him to impose Mar-a-Lago rules on the British Open. Under the Mar-a-Lago rules of golf, it’s OK for a “winner” to stomp down the grass around your ball. Hell, it’s OK to throw your ball back onto the fairway. Mar-a-Lago rules had already been invoked to rig the World Cup, so why not the Open? But the President couldn’t take my call. As the final loser, I claimed there was a conspiracy against me. Don’t tell me I don’t know something about soccer. Soccer unites the world in sore-loserism.

Advertisement

The chaotic scenes after the World Cup final – Argentine players trying to punch on and earning posthumous red cards, doddering US Presidents trying to muscle into the winner’s celebration, the eruption of conspiracy theories about the game being rigged – turned out to be completely consistent with the philosophy now embedded into global professional sport. Throughout the tournament, nobody got beaten by a better opponent. There had to be corruption or malfeasance or dark political fishiness. This great compelling carnival of sport, as it escalated to its conclusion, became more and more anti-sport. Donald Trump muscles in on Spain’s World Cup success. Getty Images “Show me a good loser, and I’ll show you a loser,” was one of the famous lines from football coach Vince Lombardi. It is a most American idea, and for the five weeks of the World Cup this American allergy to being a good loser infused the peak event of global sport. Australia was not immune, just a small-scale example. When the Socceroos lost in the round of 32 to Egypt, it was difficult to hear any credit given to the opposition or any good grace, any acknowledgement that Egypt, a soccer-mad country of 120 million, might just have a better team than Australia. Instead, commentators attacked coach Tony Popovic for his selections, the tactics of being overly defensive, and the “mentality” of lacking a killer instinct. This reaction did not show Australia to be a small soccer nation. To the contrary, it showed us to be a small version of the big soccer nations.

Advertisement

When England fell to Argentina, commentators attacked coach Thomas Tuchel for his selections, the tactics of being overly defensive, and the “mentality” of lacking a killer instinct. When France fell to Spain, ditto. When Argentina finally lost the decider, same again: coach’s selections, tactics, mentality, with the requisite addition of conspiracy theories. (Curiously, after four years of the global conspiracy theory that the World Cup was rigged for Argentina to win, the new conspiracy theory is that it was rigged for them to lose. Conspiracy theories themselves turn out to be sore losers.) Argentina and Spain players clash after full-time in the World Cup final. Getty Images Whether the sport is a billion-dollar industrial complex, a national obsessive-compulsive disorder or a third-tier, underfunded winter code, the response to defeat replicates itself: blame your own, hint at off-field shenanigans, and never, on any account, pay due credit to the other team for just being better than you on the day. Never admit that your team was forced to be “too defensive” because the other team would not let them get the ball. Never admit that the better team won. Or, if you’re Argentina, turn your backs and never even acknowledge that the other team exists. To do so might risk making you a good loser: that is, a loser. Under the hyper-magnification of the current American cultural climate, the World Cup produced this jarring, compelling mix of the very best and the very worst that sport has to offer: sublime skills and atrocious chicanery; passion so unbearable that it found its final expression in violence; the sweet purity of a 30-metre shot into the top corner against a backdrop of the filth and rot of phone calls between Donnie and Gianni. The higher the stakes, the sharper the juxtaposition.

Advertisement

If there was a game after the final, on the trajectory the World Cup was going, it would have been settled by gunfire. Maybe that’s where we’re headed in 2030, unless FIFA can break the circuit it has constructed during the past half-century. Rodri lifts the trophy as Spain celebrate their World Cup victory. Getty Images We journalists get criticised for paying too much attention to sports administrators, but the World Cup shows how administrators set the tone for the diseases that infect games. Only because of FIFA’s work over the decades does a World Cup become such fertile ground for sore-loserism: for accusations of cheating and corruption, for refusal to accept defeat, for everything that denies that a fair contest has taken place. FIFA’s naked and, under president Gianni Infantino, proud transactionalism – from ticket prices to “hydration breaks” to political favours – lays the ground for the ultimate dissatisfaction, the casting of doubt on results, the suspicion that this was not a game, it was just another transaction.

Advertisement

And yet … and yet ... Just as the de facto world championship of golf, the British Open, emerged from the DeChambeau muck to give us a winner in Ryan Fox – the most likeable and homespun individual and a deserved champion golfer of the year – the World Cup gave us Spain. Related Article Analysis

FIFA World Cup Spanish domination shows the limitations of ‘suffering’ in football What had Spain done? They’d overcome the embarrassment of their first match, when they were unable to put a goal past Cabo Verde. (Which ended up not such an embarrassment, with superhuman Cabo Verde goalkeeper Vozinha being named in the official team of the tournament despite playing just four games.) Spain had overcome the dreadful luck of a deranged draw that forced them to beat Portugal, Belgium and France before they even made it to the final. Spain had developed a brand of soccer that asphyxiated their opponents and was coldly systematic, and yet also hypnotic and, in its way, utterly pure. Spain played the best football, and then they shoved the silly old man out of their way. Football really was the winner in the end, in spite of everything FIFA could throw at it. What a dizzying month. I might not know much about football, but I know when the good guys and the best team win.

title: 2026 Census Australia: Key dates, what's included and why it matters
text:
Every five years, the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) counts every person and every household in the country as part of the Census of Population and Housing.

That includes Australians, young and old, from metropolitan and rural Australia. Even holidaymakers, international students and temporary visa holders are counted on Census night. It's often referred to as the most comprehensive snapshot of Australia, akin to a family photograph of the country.

This year, the Census will take place on Tuesday 11 August.

Emily Walter, Census national spokesperson at the ABS, said it's about more than just numbers. She believes the Census tells a story of a changing Australia.

"Our Census provides a snapshot of the country at a point in time ... So, it's really important that absolutely everyone is reflected in the Census," she told SBS Urdu.

"It is compulsory for that very good reason, and it's important that we get a very accurate count of the number of people in Australia ... because it's about providing data for the country to help serve the country."

What the Census measures

The first population count in Australia dates back to 1788. In 1911, the ABS ran its first national Census, with field officers travelling by horse or bicycle to collect information about Australians.

Generally, one person completes the Census form for the entire household. The Census can be completed online or on paper. Credit: Australian Bureau of Statistics

Today, the Census is available online and by paper and can also be completed with help from Census field staff.

It's compulsory for everyone in Australia to complete the Census. Generally, one person from each household completes the Census — although you can ask for separate forms for privacy reasons.

If an Australian is overseas on Census night, they don't need to complete the Census.

The ABS collects personal information about individuals, including age, country of birth, cultural background, living situation, work and education. Some questions about religious affiliation, gender and sexual orientation (for people aged 16 and over) will be optional.

All information collected is confidential and protected by law.

What is Census data used for?

Census data is used to inform decisions about language services, settlement support, transport, schools, health care, infrastructure and business. It also helps plan local services for individuals, families and communities.

SBS broadcasts and publishes across more than 60 languages, using data from the Census to ensure its audio, digital, and television offerings reflect the country's evolving demographics.

The data is often used by researchers to study a range of topics, including population demographics, economic trends and social issues.

The 2021 Census counted over 25 million people in Australia, excluding overseas visitors. That was an 8.6 per cent increase compared to 2016. Source: AAP

Liz Allen, a demographer at the Australian National University's Centre for Social Policy Research, said the Census provides an "important suite of information" for decision-makers.

"We've seen internationally what happens when the statistical undertaking of a Census is compromised. That means that we lose vital information, data is unable to be published ... that then leads to policymakers making decisions basically blindfolded, and it especially harms people in minority groups," she said.

She also believes the Census provides the nation with an opportunity to pause and plan for Australia's future.

"The Census for me is not just about data.

"It's about us coming together as a nation, being seen, being captured in that family photograph and ensuring that the future of this country will be data-informed and policy will reflect exactly who we are."

title: 'Life delayed': The $11,710 bill keeping some couples apart
text:
This audio is voiced by AI and may occasionally mispronounce words.

Bringing a partner to Australia has long been a costly and time-consuming process.

As of this month, applicants now face a record application fee of $11,710 — up $2,345 from the previous charge — while many continue to wait well over a year for a decision, leaving couples separated for months and, in some cases, years.

For Sarosh Akram, the increase came just as he was preparing to apply for his wife's offshore partner visa.

"It's made me think harder about how to save enough to lodge the application sooner, so I can start my wait in the Department [of Home Affairs'] queue," the 32-year-old tells SBS News.

Living in Parkes, a town in the central west of NSW, Akram is now exploring ways to cut costs and grow his savings to cover the additional amount required to apply.
